newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen rebel leader to meet Russian premier - OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Chechen rebel leader to meet Russian premier - OSCE.

text.p: Chechnya's separatist leader will meet Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in Moscow on Thursday and sign a document to further peace in the southern region, an international mediator said.

The Swiss diplomat mediating in the peace process said by telephone from the Chechen capital Grozny that the details of Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev's visit to Moscow had just been agreed between separatist and Russian representatives.

"The delegation will be leaving tomorrow morning. The meeting will be at around noon and a document will be signed," said Tim Guldimann, who heads the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe's (OSCE) Chechnya mission.
He said that Russian Security Chief Alexander Lebed, who signed a peace deal with Chechen rebel chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov in late August, would sit in on Yandarbiyev's meeting with Chernomyrdin.
Earlier on Wednesday Lebed was jeered as a "traitor" in the State Duma lower chamber of parliament and left the chamber in frustration after trying to defend agreements that ended the Chechnya war.
A rebel representative earlier told Reuters in Grozny that Yandarbiyev would fly to Moscow from the airport in neighbouring Ingushetia early on Thursday.

It would be only the second visit by the leader of the rebels who fought Russian troops for 21 months. During the first, Yandarbiyev signed a pre-election peace deal with President Boris Yeltsin which subsequently fell apart.
The new deal signed with Lebed followed some of the worst fighting in the conflict, in which tens of thousands of people have died.

A shaky ceasefire has since held, but the political aspects of deal have stirred controversy in Moscow, where some members of parliament and officials say they amount to capitulation to the rebels and could lead to the break-up of Russia.
Chernomyrdin has given cautious backing to Lebed's deal, expressing fears it could play into the hands of the rebels.

Yandarbiyev fuelled those fears in an interview with the Russian Argumenti i Fakty weekly in which he said that the deal he had signed with Lebed had confirmed Chechnya's independence and warned Moscow that the rebels would fight if necessary.
"If one side ignores bilateral relations it will bring confrontation," he said in the interview, quoted by Interfax.
A meeting between Yandarbiyev and Chernomyrdin was cast into doubt after Russian news agencies quoted government sources as saying that no such encounter was planned.
But Guldimann said separatist spokesman Movladi Udugov had confirmation from a representative of Russia's Security Council that the meeting would go ahead.
Under the deal, Moscow and the rebels agreed to postpone the issue of Chechnya's political status for five years.
But both sides have stuck by their previous positions -- the rebels pressing for independence and Moscow insisting Chechnya must stay in the Russian Federation.
